abstract: ABSTRACT Glycosylation, a crucial posttranslational modification (PTM), plays important roles in numerous biological processes and is linked to various diseases. Despite its significance, the structural complexity and diversity of glycans present significant challenges for mass spectrometry (MS)‐based quantitative analysis. This review aims to provide an in‐depth overview of recent advancements in labeling strategies for N‐glycomics and O‐glycomics, with a specific focus on enhancing the sensitivity, specificity, and throughput of MS analyses. We categorize these advancements into three major areas: (1) the development of isotopic/isobaric labeling techniques that significantly improve multiplexing capacity and throughput for glycan quantification; (2) novel methods that aid in the structural elucidation of complex glycans, particularly sialylated and fucosylated glycans; and (3) labeling techniques that enhance detection ionization efficiency, separation, and sensitivity for matrix‐assisted laser desorption/ionization (MALDI)‐MS and capillary electrophoresis (CE)‐based glycan analysis. In addition, we highlight emerging trends in single‐cell glycomics and bioinformatics tools that have the potential to revolutionize glycan quantification. These developments not only expand our understanding of glycan structures and functions but also open new avenues for biomarker discovery and therapeutic applications. Through detailed discussions of methodological advancements, this review underscores the critical role of derivatization methods in advancing glycan identification and quantification.

Stable Isotope‐Based Labeling Methods for Multiplex Glycan Quantification
Stable isotope‐based labeling methods have emerged as critical tools for enhancing the accuracy and throughput of glycan quantification. By integrating isotopic labels, researchers can achieve more reliable quantification across multiple samples, reduce run‐to‐run variability, and enhance the detection of low‐abundance glycan species. This section explores the diverse range of stable isotope labeling strategies designed to overcome the unique challenges of glycan analysis. According to the quantification stage, these methods can be divided into precursor ion‐based and product ion‐based methods. Additionally, based on the method of stable isotope introduction, precursor ion‐based methods encompass metabolic, enzymatic, and chemical labeling, each offering unique advantages in isotopic incorporation, while product ion‐based techniques typically rely on chemical labeling.
We will discuss the principles and recent advances of each quantification technique according to these classifications, and all the labeling methods discussed are summarized in
Table
1
. Additionally, for comparison, we will briefly introduce label‐free quantification methods. Furthermore, this section will discuss critical issues, such as data acquisition strategies, in‐source fragmentation (ISF), and glycan unit migration problems, which significantly affect isotope‐based glycan quantification.

2.1
Limitations of Label‐Free Quantification
Label‐free quantification, the most common method for MS‐based glycan analysis, involves comparing glycan signal intensities across multiple MS runs (Scheme
1A
) [
31
]. Although this method is straightforward and requires minimal sample preparation, it is vulnerable to quantitative inaccuracies due to matrix effects, run‐to‐run variability, and sample handling inconsistencies [
34
,
41
,
42
,
43
].
SCHEME 1
Overview of methods for multiplex glycan quantification. (A) Label‐free quantification involves the comparison of glycan signal intensities across multiple runs. This method often suffers from run‐to‐run variability, which can impact quantitative accuracy. (B) Precursor ion‐based quantification employs stable isotope labeling to introduce a mass difference between light and heavy labeling. This allows for relative quantification of labeled glycans within the same run by comparing extracted ion chromatograms (XIC). Precursor labeling methods include metabolic, enzymatic, and chemical labeling. (C) Mass defect precursor ion‐based quantification utilizes small mDa level mass differences achieved by stable isotopes to distinguish between light and heavy‐labeled glycans in high‐resolution MS1 spectra. This method effectively reduces spectral complexity. The zoomed‐in view highlights how subtle mass differences can be resolved with sufficient MS resolution. (D) Product ion‐based quantification uses isobaric labeling where differently labeled glycans coelute in MS1 with the same nominal mass. Upon fragmentation in MS/MS, distinct reporter ions are released, enabling the quantification of different samples based on reporter ion intensities. This method reduces spectral complexity and allows for high‐throughput multiplexing.
To mitigate these issues, internal standard‐based quantification has been developed. This approach involves spiking a known amount of isotopically labeled glycan standard or glycoprotein standard into the sample. These isotopic standards are chemically identical to the analytes of interest, which helps normalize variations during sample preparation and instrument performance [
44
]. As a result, this method facilitates more accurate label‐free quantification and helps in distinguishing glycan isomers through standardized retention times [
45
,
46
,
47
].
However, internal standard‐based methods also face limitations. Typically, only one or a few internal standards are used, which may not represent the entire glycan population in a sample. Significant variations in ionization efficiencies across different glycans can still lead to quantification inaccuracies. And occasionally, the addition of internal standards may further complicate the quantification results [
37
]. Also, the structural complexity of glycans often makes it challenging to synthesize isotopically labeled standards for every glycan of interest [
44
].
To address these challenges, multiplex isotope labeling methods have been developed. These techniques involve labeling all released glycans with different stable isotope encoded reagents, creating distinguishable MS peaks for glycan species from different samples. Also, multiplex labeling facilitates the simultaneous analysis of multiple samples within a single run, thereby enhancing both the quantitative reliability and analytical efficiency.
2.2
Precursor Ion‐Based Quantification
Precursor ion‐based quantification differentiates between light and heavy‐labeled precursors by introducing a mass difference typically greater than 3 Da to minimize isotopic envelope interference (Scheme
1B
). Relative quantitation of these samples is achieved by comparing the extracted ion chromatograms of light and heavy precursor ions in MS1 spectra. This approach can be classified into metabolic, enzymatic, and chemical labeling based on how the isotopic labels are introduced (Scheme
1B
), as discussed in the following sections. Figure
1
summarizes these labeling methods, organized by the different stages of isotope introduction.
2.2.1
Metabolic Labeling
Metabolic labeling involves the incorporation of stable isotopes into glycoproteins in vivo via biosynthetic pathways [
1
,
38
,
48
]. This method, achieved by culturing cells or feeding animals with isotopically labeled precursors such as glutamine or glucose, allows for early‐stage isotope incorporation, thereby enhancing quantitative accuracy. However, metabolic labeling is constrained by the turnover rates of glycans within cells, often involving slow kinetics and requiring multiple cell divisions for complete labeling [
49
].
Metabolic labeling can be applied to both N‐ and O‐glycans by incorporating isotopically labeled precursors into their biosynthetic pathways. A pioneering technique in this area, Isotope Detection of Amino sugars With Glutamine (IDAWG), involves incubating cells with
15
N‐glutamine [
50
]. This approach labels all amino‐containing glycans within the hexosamine biosynthetic pathway, including GlcNAc, GalNAc, and sialic acid, achieving nearly complete
15
N incorporation into both N‐linked and O‐linked glycans within 72 h. This facilitates quantitative glycomics in cultured cells. Building on this, Jiang et al. developed the GlyProSILC method [
51
], which also labels the peptide backbone by feeding cells with media enriched in
15
N‐glutamine,
13
C
6
‐arginine, and
13
C
6
‐
15
N
2
‐lysine, allowing for simultaneous quantitative analysis of glycans, peptides, and glycopeptides, thus providing a comprehensive view of molecular changes across multiple omics layers.
Despite its advantages, IDAWG's applicability is limited to glycans containing nitrogen atoms. For example, yeast glycans, which lack amino‐containing sugars, cannot be labeled using this method [
49
]. Moreover, smaller glycans with fewer amino‐containing monosaccharides may exhibit only minor mass increases, leading to potential isotope overlap. To address these challenges, Lim and coworkers introduced the Metabolic Isotope Labeling of Polysaccharides with Isotopic Glucose (MILPIG) method, which uses
13
C‐labeled glucose to label glycans in yeast culture [
49
]. Employing 1‐
13
C‐glucose as a universal precursor through the hexosamine biosynthetic pathway, even small glycans with fewer units achieve significant mass shifts, enhancing quantification accuracy. This method has demonstrated excellent results in analyzing glycan expression changes under tunicamycin treatment in yeast and has been successfully applied to other biological systems, such as cultured rice cells (
Oryza sativa
) [
52
]. Further building on this, Pham et al. adapted MILPIG to a triplex format, employing light, medium, and heavy isotopically labeled glucose precursors for cell culture, significantly increasing the throughput of this method [
53
].
For O‐glycan analysis, innovations in metabolic labeling have led to the development of cell‐permeable O‐glycan precursors. The Isotope‐Cellular O‐glycome Reporter Amplification (ICORA) technique, pioneered by Kudelka et al., utilizes isotopically labeled GalNAc precursors: Ac
3
‐GalNAc‐Bn H
7
and its heavier variant Ac
3
‐GalNAc‐Bn D
7
[
54
]. These precursors cross the cell membrane, undergo de‐esterification in the cytosol, and are subsequently transported into the Golgi apparatus. Within the Golgi, they are modified by endogenous glycosyltransferases to yield Bn‐O‐glycans labeled with either light H7 or heavy D7, which are subsequently secreted into the culture medium. The 7 Da mass difference between the light and heavy Bn‐O‐glycans facilitates the quantification of their relative abundances. Nan et al. further enhanced this method by incorporating sialic‐acid linkage‐specific derivatization, which allows for the distinction between different sialic acid linkage isomers, providing detailed structural insights while maintaining high quantification accuracy [
55
].
2.2.2
Enzymatic Labeling
To address the slow turnover rate associated with metabolic labeling and broaden its applicability, in vitro enzymatic labeling methodologies have been developed. Enzymatic labeling is more commonly applied to N‐glycan analysis due to the availability of specific enzymes, such as PNGase F, which efficiently release N‐glycans from glycoproteins. In contrast, the enzymatic toolbox for O‐glycan analysis is more limited, as there are fewer enzymes available for O‐glycan release and glycan‐specific transferases.
A conventional approach involves the enzymatic release of N‐glycans in H₂¹⁸O, where an ¹⁸O atom is incorporated at the reducing end. However, this strategy introduces a modest 2 Da mass difference, which may lead to overlaps within isotopic clusters, complicating MS analysis [
56
,
57
,
58
]. To address these limitations, Cao et al. developed the Glycan Reducing End Dual Isotopic Labeling (GREDIL) method. This technique leverages the
18
O/
16
O enzymatic release combined with reduction by NaBH
4
/NaBD
4
, introducing a more substantial mass difference at the reducing end [
59
]. This dual isotopic labeling also stabilizes against the exchanges between
18
O/
16
O during the conversion of aldehydes to hemiacetal, which is crucial for enhancing the accuracy of quantitative analyses.
Parallel to developments in glycan hydrolysis‐based labeling, the transglycosylation capabilities of enzymes such as ENGase offer an alternative method for introducing stable isotopes. These enzymes can transfer isotopically labeled monosaccharides onto existing glycan structures to achieve labeling. Shi et al. introduced the Quantitation by Mutant Enzyme Reaction Stable Isotope Labeling (QMERSIL) approach, employing a mutant form of the enzyme, Endo‐M‐N175Q, specifically tailored for stable isotopic labeling through transglycosylation of N‐glycans [
60
]. This method utilizes both deuterated and nondeuterated forms of a permanently charged custom‐designed glycan, MPDPZ‐Boc‐Asn‐GlcNAc, to enhance the response of labeled glycan in MS. The introduction of the mutant enzyme significantly reduces hydrolytic activity, thereby enhancing the stability and reliability of glycan labeling. Further, Jeong and Lim employed transglycosylation with endo‐M enzyme and isotope‐labeled glucose to incorporate isotopic glucose into the reducing end of N‐glycans, providing a robust platform for the relative quantification of N‐glycans in complex biological matrices [
61
].
2.2.3
Chemical Labeling
Chemical labeling of glycans is a widely used method for introducing stable isotopes. Chemical labeling is typically performed in vitro and provides broad applicability across various sample types. Common chemical labeling methods include permethylation, reducing‐end labeling, glycosamine‐based labeling, and sialic acid‐based labeling, as summarized in Figure
2
. Isotopic labeling of glycans generally involves incorporating stable isotopes (
13
C,
15
N,
2
H, and
18
O) into the labeling reagents to create mass differences detectable at the MS1 level. Accurate quantification using chemical labeling requires normalization at the glycoprotein level and complete glycan release from glycoprotein.

For N‐glycans, the most common labeling approach involves labeling the reducing end after releasing glycans with PNGase F enzyme. In contrast, alkaline β‐elimination is often used for O‐glycan release, but this process is prone to peeling side reactions, where monosaccharide units degrade during release. To address this issue, simultaneous labeling of the reducing end during chemical release is employed. Reagents such as 1‐phenyl‐3‐methyl‐5‐pyrazolone (PMP) are used to stabilize O‐glycans, preventing degradation and improving detection in MS [
30
].
In recent years, novel labeling techniques have been developed for quantitative glycan analysis. Here, we highlight the advancements post‐2020. For a more comprehensive overview, we recommend the recent review by Yun et al. [
38
] and Helali and Delporte [
39
].
For N‐glycan analysis, Wang et al. introduced a method that combines dual isotopic labeling with fluorous solid‐phase extraction (FSPE) for the simultaneous enrichment and quantification of neutral and sialylated N‐glycans in gastric cancer serum samples [
62
]. This approach uses a dual‐functional tag, O‐(2,3,4,5,6‐pentafluorobenzyl) hydroxylamine (PFBHA) and its deuterated form (PFBHA‐d2), to label the reducing ends. This not only introduces a mass difference but also enhances the selective enrichment of glycans from complex biological samples. Additionally, isotopic methylamine (MA) is used to label sialic acid residues, providing extra mass difference for sialylated glycans. These mass differences facilitate the easy identification and quantification of sialic acid‐containing glycans.
For O‐glycan quantification, Li et al. developed the O‐GlycoIsoQuant method. This technique uses the organic superbase 1,8‐diazabicyclo[5.4.0]undec‐7‐ene (DBU) combined with light and heavy isotopic Girard P reagents, achieving rapid and effective nonreductive β‐elimination to release O‐glycans from glycoproteins (Figure
3A
) [
63
]. Hydroxylamine is employed during glycan release to prevent peeling side reactions (Figure
3B
). This method enables relative quantification of O‐glycans and has shown broad applicability in complex samples such as human serum, saliva, and extracellular vesicles from human urine.

Simultaneous quantification of N‐ and O‐glycans presents significant analytical challenges as they require different release and labeling methods. To address this, Li et al. developed a method using Pronase E digestion to hydrolyze glycopeptides into single amino acids, thereby releasing both N‐ and O‐linked glycans without traditional glycan release methods [
64
,
65
]. The resultant N‐glycan‐Asn and O‐glycan‐Ser/Thr structures feature a single amino reactive group and can be labeled with designed amino‐reactive probe 3‐benzoyl‐2‐oxothiazolidine‐4‐carboxylic acid (BOTC) and its heavy version with five deuterium (Figure
3C
). This method was successfully employed in identifying 13 glycans in cetuximab antibody and in the discovery of differentially expressed glycans as potential biomarkers for acute myocardial infarction.
2.2.4
Mass Defect‐Based Chemical Labeling
Mass defect‐based quantification is an innovative technique enabling multiplexed MS1‐level precursor quantification without increasing spectral complexity (Scheme
1C
) [
1
,
66
]. This method exploits small mDa mass differences arising from nuclear binding energy differences between isotopes, known as mass defects. Samples are labeled with the same number of heavy isotopes but in unique elemental compositions and isotope configurations, resulting in distinct masses that differ at the mDa level. This isotopic mass defect on the precursor ions is indistinguishable at low resolution but can be differentiated and used for quantification via high‐resolution MS1 scans. Although its recent applications have been mainly demonstrated in N‐glycan analysis with chemical labeling, this method has potential for broader applications, including O‐glycan analysis and metabolite labeling.
The first application of mass defect‐based quantification in N‐glycomics, termed “Quantitation by Isobaric Labeling”, was demonstrated by Atwood et al. [
41
]. They showed that permethylation of glycans with
13
CH
3
I or
12
CH
2
DI introduces a 2.922 mDa mass difference per methylation site, requiring an MS resolving power of 30 K to distinguish light‐ and heavy‐labeled glycans on a hybrid LTQ‐FTICR instrument. Recently, Dong et al. expanded this strategy to 8‐plex labeling with various iodomethane reagents with a required resolution of 100 K (at
m
/

= 400) [
36
]. However, in this method, the mass shift for each glycan pair varies with the number of hydroxyl and carboxylic groups in the glycan, complicating data analysis. Additionally, multiple deuterium atoms introduced in the labeling process can cause significant retention time shifts when using the C18 column for separation.
To address these limitations, Chen et al. introduced dimethyl pyrimidinyl ornithine (DiPyrO) tags [
67
], which react with the amine group of N‐glycosylamine, ensuring consistent mass shifts and efficient labeling. These tags incorporate stable isotopes that create a 45.3 mDa mass difference, which is resolvable at 500 K resolution (at
m

= 200). This technique was applied to compare N‐glycan profiles in serum proteins from acute lymphoblastic leukemia patients before and after chemotherapy, revealing a general decrease in N‐glycan abundance postchemotherapy. Feng et al. recently developed triplex mass‐defect‐based isobaric multiplex reagents for carbonyl‐containing compounds (md‐SUGAR) [
68
]. By performing periodate oxidation on sialic acids to generate additional labeling sites, the mass difference was enlarged with multiplex labeling. They achieved baseline separation of triplex peaks at a resolution of 500 K (at
m

= 200). Labeling on sialic acids also improved MS/MS fragmentation for better structural elucidation. Interestingly, while multiple deuterium atoms were introduced, the retention time shift under hydrophilic interaction chromatography (HILIC) separation was negligible compared to C18 columns.
Compared to traditional isotopic quantification, mass defect‐based labeling allows multiplexed quantification using small mass differences without increasing spectral complexity. However, it requires MS instruments with extremely high resolution, imposing high demands on instrument performance. Also, in Orbitrap‐based instruments, space charge effects can lead to peak coalescence due to high ion density of similar mass, distorting the electric field and causing peak overlapping [
69
]. To mitigate this, the Automatic Gain Control (AGC) target must be carefully optimized: high AGC target can exacerbate ion coalescence, while low target may reduce sensitivity [
67
,
68
]. As MS resolution continues to improve, mass defect labels will see broader application and higher throughput in the future.
2.3
Product Ion‐Based Quantification
Product ion‐based quantification utilizes isobaric labeling strategies to enable the quantification of glycans at the MS/MS level (Scheme
1D
). Glycans from different samples are tagged with various isobaric channels and then mixed for downstream MS analysis. Due to the identical mass and composition of the isobaric tags, the labeled glycans will show as a single peak in the MS1 analysis. During MS/MS fragmentation, distinct reporter ions are released, enabling the quantification based on the intensity of these diagnostic ions. This method reduces MS1 spectral complexity by producing a single composite peak from different labeled samples, thereby facilitating high‐throughput quantification without increasing spectrum complexity.
Early applications of isobaric labeling focused on N‐glycans, but several challenges emerged. Most isobaric tags were initially developed for proteomics, utilizing amide‐based structures to generate reporter ions in MS/MS, such as the commonly employed tandem mass tags (TMT). However, glycosidic bonds are more labile than amide bonds and require less energy to fragment. Consequently, TMT does not efficiently produce reporter ions in MS/MS, particularly for glycans with large structures and higher branching [
37
,
70
,
71
,
72
]. Early attempts, such as NHS‐ester‐based TMT reacting with glycosamines or aminoxyTMT forming oximes with the reducing end, yielded poor quantification accuracy, low dynamic range, and high missing values during reporter ion‐based quantification [
73
,
74
].
Improved strategies include using glycan sodium adduct ions to enhance MS/MS reporter ion yield. Zhou et al. dissolved glycan samples in 0.2 M sodium chloride solution to promote the formation of sodium adduct precursor ions, observing improved quantification accuracy with aminoxyTMT reporter ions while preserving glycan structural ions for identification [
37
]. However, sodium peaks complicate the MS spectrum, and sodium ions can also affect the sensitivity of MS. Chen et al. introduced the targeted Multi‐Notch MS3 method, which involved additional MS3 fragmentation of tag‐containing structural ions to improve reporter ion yield [
71
]. However, this method requires an extra duty cycle and is only implementable on Orbitrap Tribrid MS instruments. Chen et al. also reported enhanced reporter ion signals under high collision energy but noted the complete loss of glycan structural ions due to excessive fragmentation energy. This suggests that a stepped higher‐energy collision‐induced dissociation (HCD) strategy could be a potential solution, which can collect glycan structural ions at low energy and reporter ions at high energy, achieving structural identification and quantification simultaneously.
Furthermore, modifying the structural design of isobaric tags can significantly enhance the yield of reporter ions. Yang et al. developed QUANTITY (Quaternary Amine Containing Isobaric Tag for Glycan) tags featuring a quaternary amine structure as a reporter group [
70
]. Compared to the amide structure of TMT, quaternary amine fragments more easily under low collision energy. QUANTITY‐tagged glycans produce strong structural fragments while also generating high‐yield reporter ions for precise quantification. Additionally, quaternary amine derivatization equips glycans with a permanent charge that enhances their ionization efficiency. Feng et al. developed isobaric multiplex reagents for carbonyl‐containing compounds, termed SUGAR tags, for the quantitative analysis of N‐glycans [
75
]. These tags leverage

76
,
77

Isobaric labeling strategies outperform traditional MS1‐based quantification methods in throughput and generate less complex MS1 spectra. However, isobaric labeling suffers from the inherent ratio compression problem. This phenomenon occurs when coeluting ions are co‐isolated and fragmented within the mass isolation window. The reporter ions from contaminating precursors are indistinguishable from those of the target analyte, thus compromising the accuracy of quantification [
81
]. In the context of glycans, different glycan compositions can produce similar mass. For instance, the mass of one Neu5Gc and one Fucose (453.14 Da) is identical to that of one hexose plus one Neu5Ac, and the mass of two fucoses (292.11 Da) closely resembles that of one Neu5Ac (291.09 Da) [
82
,
83
]. These mass similarities necessitate the implementation of advanced glycan separation techniques to avoid the co‐isolation of different glycan precursors when the isobaric labeling strategy is employed.

To bridge the gap between targeted and discovery‐based research, a mass signature‐guided MS/MS method has been developed. This method employs isotopic labeling and mixes light/heavy labeled glycans in a fixed ratio, then screens for unique isotope patterns generated in MS to trigger MS/MS online or generate inclusion lists for targeted analysis. 2.5
Unique Challenges in Glycan Quantification: In‐Source Fragmentation and Glycounits Migration
The quantification of glycans in MS is hindered by inherent challenges such as in‐source fragmentation (ISF) and glycan unit migration. Glycosidic bonds in glycans are inherently labile, rendering them susceptible to ISF within ion sources [
92
,
93
,
94
]. For example, MALDI‐based analysis often leads to a substantial loss of sialic acids and sulfate groups from glycans. Although ESI is considered softer than MALDI, studies have reported that about 0.2%–3% of neutral N‐glycans and more than 50% of sialylated N‐glycans dissociate into smaller fragments due to ISF under typical ESI operating conditions [
93
,
95
].
ISF can significantly impact the quantification of glycans. On one hand, the loss of sialic acids can decrease the MS signal of sialylated glycans. Detecting sialylated glycans using MALDI has long been a challenge [
96
]. On the other hand, C‐ and Y‐type fragment ions produced by ISF will have the same
m
/
z
and identical MS/MS fragments as inherent N‐glycan ions, leading to the potential misidentification of glycan species (Figure
5
) [
93
]. This interference occurs both in native N‐glycans and those with reducing‐end derivatizations [
95
]. More critically, when isotopic labeling strategies were applied, ISF‐generated glycan ions may carry the same isotopic labeling information as the parent ions, including light/heavy labels at the MS1 level and reporter ions at the MS/MS level, leading to erroneous quantitative information.

. Additionally, optimized MS ion source parameters can reduce ISF effects. Hecht et al. demonstrated that reducing the spray voltage and adjusting capillary temperatures can minimize thermal decomposition during sample introduction, improving ion production efficiency and reducing ISF in INLIGHT‐labeled glycans [
101
]. Furthermore, coupling MS with separation techniques (e.g., LC) can differentiate intact glycans from ISF‐generated ions based on retention time differences. However, due to the complex and isomeric nature of glycan structures, complete separation is often difficult [
93
]. Therefore, careful determination of peak integration areas during glycan quantitative data processing is essential to exclude signals generated by ISF, especially for isotope‐labeled glycans.
Another challenge in glycan analysis is glycounits migrations. In MS‐based glycan analysis, glycan unit migrations refer to the rearrangement of monosaccharide units, such as fucose or hexose, within the glycan structure, resulting in misleading fragment ions [
102
]. These migrations are particularly problematic for structural elucidation and quantification.
Fucose is particularly prone to migration. Fucose residues can transfer between glycan antennae or migrate to nucleophilic sites, such as the acetamido groups in GlcNAc and sialic acid [
103
,
104
]. These rearrangements are especially prominent in protonated glycan species during MS/MS, causing internal residue losses (IRLs) that mimic native glycan fragments, complicating the interpretation of MS/MS data. For instance, this can lead to false assignments of difucosylated antennae or incorrect identification of glycan epitopes such as Lewis Y [
104
].
Similarly, hexose rearrangements can complicate the analysis of reductively aminated glycans. Oligomannosidic N‐glycans, for example, frequently display hexose transfers to the innermost GlcNAc residue during MS/MS, leading to the appearance of Y‐type ions that contain additional hexoses, which are not part of the original glycan structure [
105
]. These long‐distance migrations can significantly compromise the structural interpretation and quantification of glycans.
To mitigate these effects, chemical derivatization methods such as permethylation of glycans can help prevent rearrangements by stabilizing labile glycosidic linkages [
106
]. In addition, optimizing MS settings, such as using sodium adducts instead of protonated species, can also reduce rearrangements [
104
]. Furthermore, the use of IMS has been shown to distinguish between native and rearranged glycan ions based on their different collision cross‐section (CCS) values, thus aiding in the accurate assignment of glycan structures [
103
].
In summary, understanding and mitigating the effects of ISF and glycan unit migrations are essential for accurate glycan quantification and structural analysis in MS. Implementing strategies such as chemical derivatization, optimizing instrument parameters, and employing advanced separation techniques can significantly improve data quality and reliability of glycan analysis.

N‐ and O‐glycans are two primary types of glycans, classified based on their attachment sites on proteins. N‐glycans attach to the asparagine residue within the Asn‐X‐Ser/Thr sequence (where X is any amino acid except proline), while O‐glycans attach to serine or threonine residues without a specific consensus sequence [

,
28

Mass spectrometry (MS)‐based analytical strategies enable comprehensive and sensitive analysis of glycans. High‐resolution MS precisely identifies glycan compositions by accurate mass matching, while tandem MS (MS/MS) provides detailed structural insights via various fragmentation technologies [
4
]. The standard workflow for glycan analysis with MS typically involves the release of glycans, followed by their purification, chemical derivatization (optional), separation, and MS detection (Figure

). For N‐glycans, peptide‐N‐glycosidase F (PNGase F) enzyme is commonly employed for universal release, except for a‐(1,3)‐linked core fucose glycans where PNGase A is required [

30
]. Following the release, glycans need to be enriched and purified to facilitate MS analysis, employing enrichment and separation methods such as porous graphitized carbon (PGC), and hydrophilic interaction liquid chromatography (HILIC) due to their affinity for diverse glycan structures [
31
]. In MS, soft ionization techniques, such as matrix‐assisted laser desorption/ionization (MALDI) and electrospray ionization (ESI), are commonly used for glycan analysis. Separation techniques such as liquid chromatography (LC) and capillary electrophoresis (CE) are commonly coupled with ESI‐MS, allowing for the effective separation of glycans and their isomers [
4
,
31

Stable isotope‐based labeling methods have emerged as critical tools for enhancing the accuracy and throughput of glycan quantification. By integrating isotopic labels, researchers can achieve more reliable quantification across multiple samples, reduce run‐to‐run variability, and enhance the detection of low‐abundance glycan species. This section explores the diverse range of stable isotope labeling strategies designed to overcome the unique challenges of glycan analysis. According to the quantification stage, these methods can be divided into precursor ion‐based and product ion‐based methods. Additionally, based on the method of stable isotope introduction, precursor ion‐based methods encompass metabolic, enzymatic, and chemical labeling, each offering unique advantages in isotopic incorporation, while product ion‐based techniques typically rely on chemical labeling.

2.1
Limitations of Label‐Free Quantification
Label‐free quantification, the most common method for MS‐based glycan analysis, involves comparing glycan signal intensities across multiple MS runs (Scheme
1A
) [
31
]. Although this method is straightforward and requires minimal sample preparation, it is vulnerable to quantitative inaccuracies due to matrix effects, run‐to‐run variability, and sample handling inconsistencies [
34
,
41
,
42
,
43
].

To mitigate these issues, internal standard‐based quantification has been developed. This approach involves spiking a known amount of isotopically labeled glycan standard or glycoprotein standard into the sample. These isotopic standards are chemically identical to the analytes of interest, which helps normalize variations during sample preparation and instrument performance [
44
]. As a result, this method facilitates more accurate label‐free quantification and helps in distinguishing glycan isomers through standardized retention times [
45
,
46
,
47
].
However, internal standard‐based methods also face limitations. Typically, only one or a few internal standards are used, which may not represent the entire glycan population in a sample. Significant variations in ionization efficiencies across different glycans can still lead to quantification inaccuracies. And occasionally, the addition of internal standards may further complicate the quantification results [
37
]. Also, the structural complexity of glycans often makes it challenging to synthesize isotopically labeled standards for every glycan of interest [
44
].
To address these challenges, multiplex isotope labeling methods have been developed. These techniques involve labeling all released glycans with different stable isotope encoded reagents, creating distinguishable MS peaks for glycan species from different samples. Also, multiplex labeling facilitates the simultaneous analysis of multiple samples within a single run, thereby enhancing both the quantitative reliability and analytical efficiency.
2.2
Precursor Ion‐Based Quantification
Precursor ion‐based quantification differentiates between light and heavy‐labeled precursors by introducing a mass difference typically greater than 3 Da to minimize isotopic envelope interference (Scheme
1B
). Relative quantitation of these samples is achieved by comparing the extracted ion chromatograms of light and heavy precursor ions in MS1 spectra. This approach can be classified into metabolic, enzymatic, and chemical labeling based on how the isotopic labels are introduced (Scheme
1B
), as discussed in the following sections. Figure
1
summarizes these labeling methods, organized by the different stages of isotope introduction.
2.2.1
Metabolic Labeling
Metabolic labeling involves the incorporation of stable isotopes into glycoproteins in vivo via biosynthetic pathways [
1
,
38
,
48
]. This method, achieved by culturing cells or feeding animals with isotopically labeled precursors such as glutamine or glucose, allows for early‐stage isotope incorporation, thereby enhancing quantitative accuracy. However, metabolic labeling is constrained by the turnover rates of glycans within cells, often involving slow kinetics and requiring multiple cell divisions for complete labeling [
49
].
Metabolic labeling can be applied to both N‐ and O‐glycans by incorporating isotopically labeled precursors into their biosynthetic pathways. A pioneering technique in this area, Isotope Detection of Amino sugars With Glutamine (IDAWG), involves incubating cells with
15
N‐glutamine [
50
]. This approach labels all amino‐containing glycans within the hexosamine biosynthetic pathway, including GlcNAc, GalNAc, and sialic acid, achieving nearly complete
15
N incorporation into both N‐linked and O‐linked glycans within 72 h. This facilitates quantitative glycomics in cultured cells. Building on this, Jiang et al. developed the GlyProSILC method [
51
], which also labels the peptide backbone by feeding cells with media enriched in
15
N‐glutamine,
13

13

‐lysine, allowing for simultaneous quantitative analysis of glycans, peptides, and glycopeptides, thus providing a comprehensive view of molecular changes across multiple omics layers.
Despite its advantages, IDAWG's applicability is limited to glycans containing nitrogen atoms. For example, yeast glycans, which lack amino‐containing sugars, cannot be labeled using this method [
49
]. Moreover, smaller glycans with fewer amino‐containing monosaccharides may exhibit only minor mass increases, leading to potential isotope overlap. To address these challenges, Lim and coworkers introduced the Metabolic Isotope Labeling of Polysaccharides with Isotopic Glucose (MILPIG) method, which uses
13

49

This method has demonstrated excellent results in analyzing glycan expression changes under tunicamycin treatment in yeast and has been successfully applied to other biological systems, such as cultured rice cells (
Oryza sativa

53
].
For O‐glycan analysis, innovations in metabolic labeling have led to the development of cell‐permeable O‐glycan precursors. The Isotope‐Cellular O‐glycome Reporter Amplification (ICORA) technique, pioneered by Kudelka et al., utilizes isotopically labeled GalNAc precursors: Ac

Within the Golgi, they are modified by endogenous glycosyltransferases to yield Bn‐O‐glycans labeled with either light H7 or heavy D7, which are subsequently secreted into the culture medium. The 7 Da mass difference between the light and heavy Bn‐O‐glycans facilitates the quantification of their relative abundances. Nan et al. further enhanced this method by incorporating sialic‐acid linkage‐specific derivatization, which allows for the distinction between different sialic acid linkage isomers, providing detailed structural insights while maintaining high quantification accuracy [

].
2.2.2
Enzymatic Labeling
To address the slow turnover rate associated with metabolic labeling and broaden its applicability, in vitro enzymatic labeling methodologies have been developed. Enzymatic labeling is more commonly applied to N‐glycan analysis due to the availability of specific enzymes, such as PNGase F, which efficiently release N‐glycans from glycoproteins. In contrast, the enzymatic toolbox for O‐glycan analysis is more limited, as there are fewer enzymes available for O‐glycan release and glycan‐specific transferases.
A conventional approach involves the enzymatic release of N‐glycans in H₂¹⁸O, where an ¹⁸O atom is incorporated at the reducing end. However, this strategy introduces a modest 2 Da mass difference, which may lead to overlaps within isotopic clusters, complicating MS analysis [
56
,
57
,
58
]. To address these limitations, Cao et al. developed the Glycan Reducing End Dual Isotopic Labeling (GREDIL) method. This technique leverages the
18
O/
16
O enzymatic release combined with reduction by NaBH
4
/NaBD
4
, introducing a more substantial mass difference at the reducing end [
59
]. This dual isotopic labeling also stabilizes against the exchanges between
18
O/
16
O during the conversion of aldehydes to hemiacetal, which is crucial for enhancing the accuracy of quantitative analyses.
Parallel to developments in glycan hydrolysis‐based labeling, the transglycosylation capabilities of enzymes such as ENGase offer an alternative method for introducing stable isotopes. These enzymes can transfer isotopically labeled monosaccharides onto existing glycan structures to achieve labeling. Shi et al. introduced the Quantitation by Mutant Enzyme Reaction Stable Isotope Labeling (QMERSIL) approach, employing a mutant form of the enzyme, Endo‐M‐N175Q, specifically tailored for stable isotopic labeling through transglycosylation of N‐glycans [
60
]. This method utilizes both deuterated and nondeuterated forms of a permanently charged custom‐designed glycan, MPDPZ‐Boc‐Asn‐GlcNAc, to enhance the response of labeled glycan in MS. The introduction of the mutant enzyme significantly reduces hydrolytic activity, thereby enhancing the stability and reliability of glycan labeling. Further, Jeong and Lim employed transglycosylation with endo‐M enzyme and isotope‐labeled glucose to incorporate isotopic glucose into the reducing end of N‐glycans, providing a robust platform for the relative quantification of N‐glycans in complex biological matrices [
61
].

Chemical labeling of glycans is a widely used method for introducing stable isotopes. Chemical labeling is typically performed in vitro and provides broad applicability across various sample types. Common chemical labeling methods include permethylation, reducing‐end labeling, glycosamine‐based labeling, and sialic acid‐based labeling, as summarized in Figure

For N‐glycans, the most common labeling approach involves labeling the reducing end after releasing glycans with PNGase F enzyme. In contrast, alkaline β‐elimination is often used for O‐glycan release, but this process is prone to peeling side reactions, where monosaccharide units degrade during release. To address this issue, simultaneous labeling of the reducing end during chemical release is employed. Reagents such as 1‐phenyl‐3‐methyl‐5‐pyrazolone (PMP) are used to stabilize O‐glycans, preventing degradation and improving detection in MS [
30
].
In recent years, novel labeling techniques have been developed for quantitative glycan analysis. Here, we highlight the advancements post‐2020. For a more comprehensive overview, we recommend the recent review by Yun et al. [
38
] and Helali and Delporte [
39
].
For N‐glycan analysis, Wang et al. introduced a method that combines dual isotopic labeling with fluorous solid‐phase extraction (FSPE) for the simultaneous enrichment and quantification of neutral and sialylated N‐glycans in gastric cancer serum samples [
62
]. This approach uses a dual‐functional tag, O‐(2,3,4,5,6‐pentafluorobenzyl) hydroxylamine (PFBHA) and its deuterated form (PFBHA‐d2), to label the reducing ends. This not only introduces a mass difference but also enhances the selective enrichment of glycans from complex biological samples. Additionally, isotopic methylamine (MA) is used to label sialic acid residues, providing extra mass difference for sialylated glycans. These mass differences facilitate the easy identification and quantification of sialic acid‐containing glycans.
For O‐glycan quantification, Li et al. developed the O‐GlycoIsoQuant method. This technique uses the organic superbase 1,8‐diazabicyclo[5.4.0]undec‐7‐ene (DBU) combined with light and heavy isotopic Girard P reagents, achieving rapid and effective nonreductive β‐elimination to release O‐glycans from glycoproteins (Figure
3A
) [
63
]. Hydroxylamine is employed during glycan release to prevent peeling side reactions (Figure
3B
). This method enables relative quantification of O‐glycans and has shown broad applicability in complex samples such as human serum, saliva, and extracellular vesicles from human urine.

To address this, Li et al. developed a method using Pronase E digestion to hydrolyze glycopeptides into single amino acids, thereby releasing both N‐ and O‐linked glycans without traditional glycan release methods [

2.2.4
Mass Defect‐Based Chemical Labeling
Mass defect‐based quantification is an innovative technique enabling multiplexed MS1‐level precursor quantification without increasing spectral complexity (Scheme
1C
) [
1
,
66
]. This method exploits small mDa mass differences arising from nuclear binding energy differences between isotopes, known as mass defects. Samples are labeled with the same number of heavy isotopes but in unique elemental compositions and isotope configurations, resulting in distinct masses that differ at the mDa level. This isotopic mass defect on the precursor ions is indistinguishable at low resolution but can be differentiated and used for quantification via high‐resolution MS1 scans. Although its recent applications have been mainly demonstrated in N‐glycan analysis with chemical labeling, this method has potential for broader applications, including O‐glycan analysis and metabolite labeling.
The first application of mass defect‐based quantification in N‐glycomics, termed “Quantitation by Isobaric Labeling”, was demonstrated by Atwood et al. [
41
]. They showed that permethylation of glycans with
13
CH
3
I or
12
CH
2
DI introduces a 2.922 mDa mass difference per methylation site, requiring an MS resolving power of 30 K to distinguish light‐ and heavy‐labeled glycans on a hybrid LTQ‐FTICR instrument. Recently, Dong et al. expanded this strategy to 8‐plex labeling with various iodomethane reagents with a required resolution of 100 K (at
m
/
z
= 400) [
36
]. However, in this method, the mass shift for each glycan pair varies with the number of hydroxyl and carboxylic groups in the glycan, complicating data analysis. Additionally, multiple deuterium atoms introduced in the labeling process can cause significant retention time shifts when using the C18 column for separation.
To address these limitations, Chen et al. introduced dimethyl pyrimidinyl ornithine (DiPyrO) tags [
67
], which react with the amine group of N‐glycosylamine, ensuring consistent mass shifts and efficient labeling. These tags incorporate stable isotopes that create a 45.3 mDa mass difference, which is resolvable at 500 K resolution (at
m
/
z
= 200). This technique was applied to compare N‐glycan profiles in serum proteins from acute lymphoblastic leukemia patients before and after chemotherapy, revealing a general decrease in N‐glycan abundance postchemotherapy. Feng et al. recently developed triplex mass‐defect‐based isobaric multiplex reagents for carbonyl‐containing compounds (md‐SUGAR) [
68
]. By performing periodate oxidation on sialic acids to generate additional labeling sites, the mass difference was enlarged with multiplex labeling. They achieved baseline separation of triplex peaks at a resolution of 500 K (at
m
/
z
= 200). Labeling on sialic acids also improved MS/MS fragmentation for better structural elucidation. Interestingly, while multiple deuterium atoms were introduced, the retention time shift under hydrophilic interaction chromatography (HILIC) separation was negligible compared to C18 columns.
Compared to traditional isotopic quantification, mass defect‐based labeling allows multiplexed quantification using small mass differences without increasing spectral complexity. However, it requires MS instruments with extremely high resolution, imposing high demands on instrument performance. Also, in Orbitrap‐based instruments, space charge effects can lead to peak coalescence due to high ion density of similar mass, distorting the electric field and causing peak overlapping [
69
]. To mitigate this, the Automatic Gain Control (AGC) target must be carefully optimized: high AGC target can exacerbate ion coalescence, while low target may reduce sensitivity [
67
,
68
]. As MS resolution continues to improve, mass defect labels will see broader application and higher throughput in the future.
2.3
Product Ion‐Based Quantification
Product ion‐based quantification utilizes isobaric labeling strategies to enable the quantification of glycans at the MS/MS level (Scheme
1D
). Glycans from different samples are tagged with various isobaric channels and then mixed for downstream MS analysis. Due to the identical mass and composition of the isobaric tags, the labeled glycans will show as a single peak in the MS1 analysis. During MS/MS fragmentation, distinct reporter ions are released, enabling the quantification based on the intensity of these diagnostic ions. This method reduces MS1 spectral complexity by producing a single composite peak from different labeled samples, thereby facilitating high‐throughput quantification without increasing spectrum complexity.
Early applications of isobaric labeling focused on N‐glycans, but several challenges emerged. Most isobaric tags were initially developed for proteomics, utilizing amide‐based structures to generate reporter ions in MS/MS, such as the commonly employed tandem mass tags (TMT). However, glycosidic bonds are more labile than amide bonds and require less energy to fragment. Consequently, TMT does not efficiently produce reporter ions in MS/MS, particularly for glycans with large structures and higher branching [
37
,
70
,
71
,
72
]. Early attempts, such as NHS‐ester‐based TMT reacting with glycosamines or aminoxyTMT forming oximes with the reducing end, yielded poor quantification accuracy, low dynamic range, and high missing values during reporter ion‐based quantification [
73
,
74
].
Improved strategies include using glycan sodium adduct ions to enhance MS/MS reporter ion yield. Zhou et al. dissolved glycan samples in 0.2 M sodium chloride solution to promote the formation of sodium adduct precursor ions, observing improved quantification accuracy with aminoxyTMT reporter ions while preserving glycan structural ions for identification [
37
]. However, sodium peaks complicate the MS spectrum, and sodium ions can also affect the sensitivity of MS. Chen et al. introduced the targeted Multi‐Notch MS3 method, which involved additional MS3 fragmentation of tag‐containing structural ions to improve reporter ion yield [
71
]. However, this method requires an extra duty cycle and is only implementable on Orbitrap Tribrid MS instruments. Chen et al. also reported enhanced reporter ion signals under high collision energy but noted the complete loss of glycan structural ions due to excessive fragmentation energy. This suggests that a stepped higher‐energy collision‐induced dissociation (HCD) strategy could be a potential solution, which can collect glycan structural ions at low energy and reporter ions at high energy, achieving structural identification and quantification simultaneously.
Furthermore, modifying the structural design of isobaric tags can significantly enhance the yield of reporter ions. Yang et al. developed QUANTITY (Quaternary Amine Containing Isobaric Tag for Glycan) tags featuring a quaternary amine structure as a reporter group [
70
]. Compared to the amide structure of TMT, quaternary amine fragments more easily under low collision energy. QUANTITY‐tagged glycans produce strong structural fragments while also generating high‐yield reporter ions for precise quantification. Additionally, quaternary amine derivatization equips glycans with a permanent charge that enhances their ionization efficiency. Feng et al. developed isobaric multiplex reagents for carbonyl‐containing compounds, termed SUGAR tags, for the quantitative analysis of N‐glycans [
75
]. These tags leverage
N
,
N
‐dimethyl leucine as the reporter group, which demonstrates better efficiency in reporter ion generation compared with TMT [
76
,
77
]. Reporter ion intensity from SUGAR‐tagged acidic N‐glycan was found to be more than fourfold higher upon fragmentation compared with sample glycan labeled with AminoxyTMT. Initially configured as a 4‐plex system with a 1 Da spacing between reporter ions, the SUGAR tags have recently evolved into a 12‐plex format [
78
]. This expansion of quantitation capacity was achieved by incorporating diverse heavy isotopes into the reporter group, resulting in unique combinations of
13
C,
2
H, and
15
N isotopes that create 5.8 mDa mass differences between the reporter ions. This design allows for precise N‐glycan quantification of 12 samples at MS/MS resolutions exceeding 60 K (at
m
/
z
= 200), significantly improving throughput in quantitative glycomics studies.
For the quantification of O‐glycans, the
N
,
N
‐dimethyl leucine‐based isobaric tag was recently developed. Li et al. developed the DiLeu‐PMP (
N
,
N
‐dimethyl leucine‐containing pyrazolone analog) tags, which integrate the DiLeu reporter group into the PMP benzoic ring structure [
79
]. PMP derivatization was used to suppress side reactions during the β‐elimination release of O‐glycans, such as peeling degradation [
80
]. This innovative structure combines the release and isobaric labeling of O‐glycans in a single step, facilitating high‐throughput quantitative analysis. The stability and efficiency of this method have been validated through its application to complex biological samples, including human serum, demonstrating excellent performance in analyzing O‐glycans.
Isobaric labeling strategies outperform traditional MS1‐based quantification methods in throughput and generate less complex MS1 spectra. However, isobaric labeling suffers from the inherent ratio compression problem. This phenomenon occurs when coeluting ions are co‐isolated and fragmented within the mass isolation window. The reporter ions from contaminating precursors are indistinguishable from those of the target analyte, thus compromising the accuracy of quantification [
81
]. In the context of glycans, different glycan compositions can produce similar mass. For instance, the mass of one Neu5Gc and one Fucose (453.14 Da) is identical to that of one hexose plus one Neu5Ac, and the mass of two fucoses (292.11 Da) closely resembles that of one Neu5Ac (291.09 Da) [
82
,
83
]. These mass similarities necessitate the implementation of advanced glycan separation techniques to avoid the co‐isolation of different glycan precursors when the isobaric labeling strategy is employed.

DDA is the most frequently applied data acquisition method, selecting the most intense precursor ions during MS scans for fragmentation. This approach provides detailed insights into the most abundant glycan species. Although DDA yields high‐quality MS/MS data for these selected ions, its reliance on ion intensity means that less abundant species are often missed and ignored for MS/MS fragmentation [
84
]. This limitation is particularly impactful for methods relying on reporter ions, as the MS/MS spectra also carry the quantitative information.
Targeted acquisition complements the DDA method by focusing on specific and known glycans. Researchers predefine a glycan
m
/
z
library and select these ions for MS and MS/MS scans, achieving high sensitivity and accuracy in detecting and quantifying specific glycans. Multiple reaction monitoring (MRM) and parallel reaction monitoring (PRM) based methods have been developed in different instrument platforms [
85
,
86
]. For example, Wang et al. employed MRM to precisely quantify trace sulfated IgG N‐glycans, enabling the sensitive detection of low‐abundance glycans from patient samples, which are potential biomarkers for rheumatoid arthritis [
87
]. However, targeted analysis relies on predefined glycan targets, limiting its utility in exploratory research where unknown glycan structures may be of interest.
To bridge the gap between targeted and discovery‐based research, a mass signature‐guided MS/MS method has been developed. This method employs isotopic labeling and mixes light/heavy labeled glycans in a fixed ratio, then screens for unique isotope patterns generated in MS to trigger MS/MS online or generate inclusion lists for targeted analysis. For example, Woo et al. designed a dibrominated biotin tag to introduce a 1:2:1 mass signature on labeled unnatural glycans to guide MS/MS fragmentation [
88
]. Recently, Ma et al. reported a mdSUGAR Isobaric‐Labeling Guide Fingerprint Embedding (MAGNI) method [
84
]. This method uses a 6‐plex mdSUGAR tag that embeds a triple mass defect fingerprint into labeled glycans. Utilizing ultra‐high‐resolution MS and the in‐house developed MAGNI‐Finder software tool, glycans carrying these unique mass fingerprints can be identified in MS1 spectra (Figure
4C
). These embedded fingerprints guide the selection and fragmentation of target precursor ions and provide structural information on glycans. This approach significantly improves the repeatability compared to the DDA method while maintaining the applicability in N‐glycan discovery compared to library‐based targeted methods.
For DIA analysis, exemplified by the Sequential Window Acquisition of All Theoretical Mass Spectra (SWATH‐MS) method, fragment information from all precursor ions is captured within defined large sequential isolation windows. DIA can overcome the randomness of DDA and allows the use of MS/MS fragment ions for quantification to enhance sensitivity [
89
,
90
]. The integration of effective separation techniques, such as CE, LC, or ion mobility spectrometry (IMS), is crucial for enhancing the performance of DIA [
91
]. By reducing spectral complexity, these methods facilitate more accurate MS/MS deconvolution, overcoming challenges posed by the complex structures of glycans. Despite recent advances in DIA methods for glycopeptide quantification, its application in glycan quantification remains relatively limited.
Recently, Xie et al. introduced a glycanDIA method, which employs staggered DIA to enhance the sensitivity and reproducibility of glycan quantification [
83
]. They developed a generic search engine, GlycanDIA Finder, using iterative decoy searching to ensure reliable glycan identification from DIA data. To achieve effective glycan separation, they applied a nanoflow PGC column in their workflow. GlycanDIA effectively distinguishes the composition and isomers of glycans and reveals unique information about low‐abundance sulfated glycan modifications. Their experiments demonstrated the applicability of glycanDIA in analyzing N‐glycans, O‐glycans, and milk oligosaccharides, and notably, they successfully analyzed N‐glycans released from glycoRNA samples, which were underrepresented previously due to their low abundance.
2.5
Unique Challenges in Glycan Quantification: In‐Source Fragmentation and Glycounits Migration
The quantification of glycans in MS is hindered by inherent challenges such as in‐source fragmentation (ISF) and glycan unit migration. Glycosidic bonds in glycans are inherently labile, rendering them susceptible to ISF within ion sources [
92
,
93
,
94
]. For example, MALDI‐based analysis often leads to a substantial loss of sialic acids and sulfate groups from glycans. Although ESI is considered softer than MALDI, studies have reported that about 0.2%–3% of neutral N‐glycans and more than 50% of sialylated N‐glycans dissociate into smaller fragments due to ISF under typical ESI operating conditions [
93
,
95
].
ISF can significantly impact the quantification of glycans. On one hand, the loss of sialic acids can decrease the MS signal of sialylated glycans. Detecting sialylated glycans using MALDI has long been a challenge [
96
]. On the other hand, C‐ and Y‐type fragment ions produced by ISF will have the same
m
/
z
and identical MS/MS fragments as inherent N‐glycan ions, leading to the potential misidentification of glycan species (Figure
5
) [
93
]. This interference occurs both in native N‐glycans and those with reducing‐end derivatizations [
95
]. More critically, when isotopic labeling strategies were applied, ISF‐generated glycan ions may carry the same isotopic labeling information as the parent ions, including light/heavy labels at the MS1 level and reporter ions at the MS/MS level, leading to erroneous quantitative information.

To mitigate the effects of ISF, several derivatization strategies have been developed, including permethylation, esterification, and amidation [
97
,
98
,
99
,
100
]. These methods significantly enhance the stability of sialic acids in both MALDI and ESI and reduce ISF. These methods also enable sialic acids isomer differentiation, as will be detailed in Section
3.1
. Additionally, optimized MS ion source parameters can reduce ISF effects. Hecht et al. demonstrated that reducing the spray voltage and adjusting capillary temperatures can minimize thermal decomposition during sample introduction, improving ion production efficiency and reducing ISF in INLIGHT‐labeled glycans [
101
]. Furthermore, coupling MS with separation techniques (e.g., LC) can differentiate intact glycans from ISF‐generated ions based on retention time differences. However, due to the complex and isomeric nature of glycan structures, complete separation is often difficult [
93
]. Therefore, careful determination of peak integration areas during glycan quantitative data processing is essential to exclude signals generated by ISF, especially for isotope‐labeled glycans.
Another challenge in glycan analysis is glycounits migrations. In MS‐based glycan analysis, glycan unit migrations refer to the rearrangement of monosaccharide units, such as fucose or hexose, within the glycan structure, resulting in misleading fragment ions [
102
]. These migrations are particularly problematic for structural elucidation and quantification.
Fucose is particularly prone to migration. Fucose residues can transfer between glycan antennae or migrate to nucleophilic sites, such as the acetamido groups in GlcNAc and sialic acid [
103
,
104
]. These rearrangements are especially prominent in protonated glycan species during MS/MS, causing internal residue losses (IRLs) that mimic native glycan fragments, complicating the interpretation of MS/MS data. For instance, this can lead to false assignments of difucosylated antennae or incorrect identification of glycan epitopes such as Lewis Y [
104
].
Similarly, hexose rearrangements can complicate the analysis of reductively aminated glycans. Oligomannosidic N‐glycans, for example, frequently display hexose transfers to the innermost GlcNAc residue during MS/MS, leading to the appearance of Y‐type ions that contain additional hexoses, which are not part of the original glycan structure [
105
]. These long‐distance migrations can significantly compromise the structural interpretation and quantification of glycans.
To mitigate these effects, chemical derivatization methods such as permethylation of glycans can help prevent rearrangements by stabilizing labile glycosidic linkages [
106
]. In addition, optimizing MS settings, such as using sodium adducts instead of protonated species, can also reduce rearrangements [
104
]. Furthermore, the use of IMS has been shown to distinguish between native and rearranged glycan ions based on their different collision cross‐section (CCS) values, thus aiding in the accurate assignment of glycan structures [
103
].
In summary, understanding and mitigating the effects of ISF and glycan unit migrations are essential for accurate glycan quantification and structural analysis in MS. Implementing strategies such as chemical derivatization, optimizing instrument parameters, and employing advanced separation techniques can significantly improve data quality and reliability of glycan analysis.
3
Labeling Techniques for Improved Glycan Structure Elucidation
3.1
Derivatization of Sialic Acid
Sialic acids, a group of acidic 9‐carbon carbohydrates, are commonly located at the nonreducing ends of N‐ and O‐glycans. They predominantly cap Gal and GalNAc residues through α2,3‐ and α2,6‐linkages. Sialylated glycans play vital and unique roles in influencing a wide range of physiological and pathological processes [
24
,
107
–
109
]. Sialyl‐linkage isomers with α‐2,3 and α‐2,6 linkages are selectively recognized in certain cellular interactions and undergo dynamic changes in various pathological conditions [
110
,
111
]. This highlights the importance of elucidating glycan structures and sialylation patterns.
The presence of sialic acid residues on glycans introduces several analytical challenges in MS. The strong negative charges on sialic acids generally reduce their ionization efficiencies, resulting in biased quantification [
40
,
112
]. Moreover, sialic acids are susceptible to loss during MS due to their inherent instability [
113
]. This loss is more pronounced in MALDI‐MS than in ESI‐MS, likely due to the higher internal energy of ions generated by MALDI compared to those produced by ESI.
An early approach to enhancing MALDI‐MS analysis of sialic acid‐containing glycans involves permethylation of all carboxyl, hydroxyl, and amine groups within the glycoconjugate analyte [
33
,
96
]. Alternatively, sialic acid carboxylate groups can be selectively converted into esters or amides [
114
,
115
]. This can be accomplished by uniformly derivatizing α2,3 and α2,6 sialic acid linkage isomers using specific reagents.
Sialylated N‐glycan isomers with α‐2,3 and α‐2,6 linkages are essential in numerous physiological and pathological processes, with alterations in α‐2,3‐linked sialic acids being particularly important for tracking disease onset and progression [
116
,
117
,
118
]. However, analyzing these specific isomers is challenging due to their low abundance and the limitations of existing separation and detection techniques. To address this, Cheng et al. [
119
] developed an integrated strategy that combines linkage‐specific derivatization with charge‐sensitive separation using microfluidic chip capillary electrophoresis–MS (MCE–MS). This method specifically targets α‐2,3‐sialylated N‐glycan linkage isomers, where α‐2,6 sialic acids are selectively labeled with MA and α‐2,3 sialic acids with
N
,
N
‐dimethylethylenediamine (DMEN). Additionally, Jin et al. [
120
] introduced an analytical strategy called “glycoqueuing,” which enabled sequential chromatographic elution and high‐sensitivity MS quantification of various sialylglycan isomers. Cheng et al. [
121
] also developed a novel strategy combining one‐step sialic acid derivatization with positive charge‐sensitive separation and highly sensitive detection using MCE‐MS. By using an easily charged long‐chain amino compound for derivatization, this method allows for efficient separation of isomers within 10 min due to structural conformation differences.
3.2
Derivatization of Fucosylated Glycans
Fucosylation is a crucial structural feature of protein N‐glycans and has been identified as a potential marker for diseases [
122
,
123
]. In therapeutic proteins, such as monoclonal antibodies (mAbs), fucosylation significantly impacts a drug's efficacy and safety [
124
,
125
]. As a result, accurately identifying and detecting fucosylation is crucial for quality control in the biopharmaceutical industry. MS is among the most sensitive, rapid, and widely used techniques for analyzing fucosylated glycans. However, directly determining the position of fucose in native glycans is challenging due to its instability and extensive migration during MS/MS experiments. Although derivatization techniques can reduce fucose loss, they often introduce ambiguity and are too labor‐intensive for routine use.
Employing specific fucosidases to determine fucosylation, though effective, is often cumbersome and time‐consuming, making it impractical for routine N‐glycan analysis. As an alternative, Nwosu et al. [
126
] explored labeling N‐glycans with procainamide hydrochloride to prevent fucose migration during MS/MS analysis. A significant finding from the MS/MS data was the observation of the
m
/
z
587.3 core fucose diagnostic peak, corresponding to [GlcNAc + Fucose + Procainamide + H]
+
. Lattová et al. [
127
] proposed phenylhydrazine (PHN) labeling for the structural analysis of fucosylated N‐glycans using tandem MALDI MS in the positive ion mode.
3.3
Labeling Effect on Ion Mobility Spectrometry
The analysis of complex oligosaccharides often uses LC coupled with tandem mass spectrometry (LC‐MS/MS), but distinguishing isomers remains challenging. Ion mobility spectrometry (IMS) has shown potential as an additional tool for glycan analysis, as its time scale is compatible with LC‐MS workflows [
128
,
129
]. However, little is known about how common fluorescent labels used in LC‐MS affect IMS separations. The results from Manz et al. reveal that isomer separation varies significantly based on the label and ion type, with some labels enhancing peak resolution and aiding in isomer distinction [
130
]. By using IMS with both natural (NAT) and stable‐isotope label (SIL) from INLIGHT, the mobility alignment of labeled glycans provided greater confidence in glycan identification and enabled isomer examinations [
131
].
4
Labeling Techniques for Enhanced Ionization Efficiency, Separation, and Sensitivity
4.1
Reactive Matrix in MALDI
MALDI‐MS is commonly employed for glycomics profiling, but detecting carbohydrates using MALDI‐TOF MS often faces challenges such as poor ionization efficiency, instability, and matrix interference in the low molecular weight region [
132
]. The choice of matrix is a crucial factor that affects the sensitivity of MALDI‐based methods. 2‐Aminobenzoic acid (2‐AA) is frequently utilized to label released N‐glycans at their free‐reducing terminus via reductive amination, thereby increasing sensitivity. However, this process is labor‐intensive, time‐consuming, and often results in sample loss during cleanup. Hronowski et al. [
133
] reported a method using 2‐AA for labeling N‐glycans directly on a MALDI target via nonreductive amination, which also serves as a matrix in MALDI‐MS analysis. This method significantly increases glycan anionic signals compared to the traditional 2,5‐DHB matrix and simplifies glycan profiles.
Labeling‐based methods significantly increase the sensitivity of MALDI‐based glycome analysis. Barada and Hinou [
134
] evaluated and optimized a new solid ionic matrix composed of O‐benzylhydroxylamine (BOA), 2,5‐dihydroxybenzoic acid (DHB), and a small amount of sodium as the counter salt of DHB. This composition led to O‐benzyloxy tagging of the reducing ends of glycans on a MALDI target plate. Lin et al. [
135
] demonstrated that 2‐hydrazinoquinoline (2‐HQ) can be used as a reactive matrix to enable sensitive detection of neutral, sialic, and low molecular weight carbohydrates in both positive and negative ion modes. Liao et al. [
136
] designed and synthesized α‐cyano‐3‐aminocinnamic acid (3‐CACA) as a novel reactive matrix for N‐glycan analysis. By combining it with the traditional matrix α‐cyano‐4‐hydroxycinnamic acid (CHCA) as an acidic catalyst, the resulting 3‐CACA/CHCA matrix achieved homogeneous cocrystallization and high derivatization efficiency.
4.2
Labeling Methods for Capillary Electrophoresis‐Based Glycan Analysis
High‐resolution CE is widely used for carbohydrate separation, particularly for N‐glycans, due to its speed and efficiency. CE separates molecules based on their electrophoretic mobilities within a capillary under a high‐voltage electrical field [
137
]. CE is highly sensitive, requiring only low sample concentrations and providing high‐throughput capabilities. However, since glycans lack protonated sites, labeling methods are essential for CE‐based applications.
Khatri et al. [
138
] detailed the use of an MCE‐MS system for analyzing released glycans. They employed glycan TMT‐labeling to improve electrophoretic migration and facilitate multiplexed quantitation via MS/MS. Additionally, sialic acid linkage‐specific derivatization methods were used to enhance separation and increase the depth of information from a single analytical step. Lageveen‐Kammeijer et al. [
139
] introduced a highly sensitive method for characterizing released N‐glycans by integrating CE‐ESI‐MS with linkage‐specific derivatization of sialic acids and uniform cationic reducing end labeling of all glycans (Figure
6
). This method allows for glycan analysis at the attomole level, aids in the identification of sialic acid isomers, and enables detailed characterization of complex samples.

5
Future Trends for Glycomics Analysis
5.1
Single‐Cell Glycomics
The development of advanced single‐cell dispensers and significant enhancements in MS sensitivity have enabled proteomic profiling at the individual cell level [
142
]. However, established methods for single‐cell glycome analysis are lacking, primarily due to challenges in amplifying glycan signals and reducing sample losses during processing and labeling. Recently, Marie et al. [
143
] introduced an integrated platform combining online in‐capillary sample processing with high‐sensitivity, label‐free CE‐MS for N‐glycan profiling of single mammalian cells, as shown in Figure
7
. This platform allows for direct and unbiased quantitative characterization of single‐cell surface N‐glycomes, as demonstrated using HeLa and U87 cells, with the capability to detect up to 100 N‐glycans per single cell.

As labeling methods continue to evolve, they show great potential for enhancing the sensitivity and throughput of single‐cell glycomics analysis. The Boosting to Amplify Signal with Isobaric Labeling (BASIL) strategy, commonly employed in single‐cell proteomics, involves mixing “boosting” channel‐labeled samples with single‐cell samples to substantially improve the quantification of low‐abundance peptides through isobaric labeling [

,

]. With the expanding multiplexing capabilities of isobaric probes for glycans, BASIL strategies are poised to become feasible in single‐cell glycomics.
5.2
Software Development for Glycan Identification and Quantification
Given the high volume of samples often handled in glycomics analyses, there is a critical need for high‐throughput and reliable data processing software. Unlike proteomics, where automated data processing is routine, software for glycomics remains underdeveloped. Currently, the most accurate method for identifying glycans relies on manual processing, which is time‐consuming due to glycosylation microheterogeneity and becomes impractical with large datasets from complex biological samples. To streamline these labor‐intensive tasks, the development of computational algorithms that enable automated and precise identification and quantification of glycans is essential.
A recent significant advancement is CandyCrunch [
146
], a dilated residual neural network, which was trained on a curated set of 500,000 annotated MS/MS spectra (Figure
8
). It predicts glycan structures from raw LC‐MS/MS data within seconds, achieving an accuracy of 90.3%. An open‐access Python‐based workflow was also created for raw data conversion and prediction, including automated curation and fragment annotation. However, the algorithm is only suitable for native glycans, as the fragmentation patterns of derivatized glycans change due to derivatization.

] recently introduced GlycoHunter, a user‐friendly software developed in MATLAB designed for the precise and efficient processing of MS1 glycomics data. This tool facilitates the relative quantification of glycan pairs generated from multiplex isotopic labeling, including but not limited to INLIGHT labeling. This advancement has promoted the automation of glycan identification and data processing of multiplex labeling. However, it cannot provide MS/MS structural information, which hinders the specific structural identification of glycans. Currently, the automation of glycan identification and quantification data processing remains a significant challenge for derivatization‐based methods. Future developments are expected to produce new algorithms and software tools that are more adaptable to various glycan derivatization types, broadening applications of labeling methods in glycomics research.
5.3
Clinical Glycomics
Accurate glycome quantification is increasingly important for biological analysis, particularly in discovering disease biomarkers for prognosis and diagnosis, and understanding cell metabolism and disease pathology [
148
]. Recent advancements in MS instrumentation have improved resolution and sensitivity, enabling more reliable structural identification and glycan quantification. However, ionization variability in labeling methods can affect quantitation accuracy due to inconsistent spray quality [
149
]. In addition to analytical challenges, the application of glycomics research in clinical settings is hindered by a lack of clear clinical evidence. Although there are significant efforts to design studies with proper hypotheses, cohort selection, and method choice, these efforts should be more closely aligned with well‐defined unmet clinical needs to improve the translation of glycomics into actionable clinical parameters.
6
Conclusions
Recent advancements in labeling‐based glycomics have significantly elevated the precision, sensitivity, and throughput of MS analyses. This review provides an in‐depth examination of the core principles, applications, benefits, and limitations of various labeling strategies, covering both N‐glycomics and O‐glycomics. Each technique offers distinct advantages while also presenting certain challenges. These improvements in labeling technologies have led to more effective comparative and multiplex quantitative studies. Additionally, the continuous evolution of labeling techniques has provided researchers with cutting‐edge tools for biomarker discovery, clinical diagnosis, and even single‐cell analysis with unprecedented sensitivity. These advancements have not only deepened our understanding of glycan structures and functions but have also made glycomics analysis more accessible to the broader scientific community. As these technologies continue to advance, they are expected to unveil new molecular insights in glycomics that could lead to the discovery of novel biomarkers and therapeutic targets.
